If you love classic Star Trek and flight simulators, this game is for you!  This game is one of my favorite PC games.  I was so happy to see it on Steam!  Phasers, photons, and cloaking Oh My!  You can target individual ship systems, disabling your enemy and toy with them   >:)

I remember playing this game when it was new and coming back to it after so many years and for such a cheap price, I highly recommend Star Trek fans give this a try. There are a couple of instant game over points from story choices, so keep that in mind and make many saves.

The game uses live recordings, but with early PC gaming green screens and compression, so expect the visuals to be a bit lacking. But it's work it to see Shatner, Takei and Koenig return to their characters in the Monster Maroons. Set before Sulu takes command of the Excelsior, he is a temporary instructor for the Academy and brings the others with him. You are leading a crew of cadets while on the Command Track and running simulations, among the many missions being the famous Koboyashi Maru.

This is one of the early Trek games and I'm quite sure it is the first Flight sim Trek game being released originally in '97. Control's are not too hard to get to grips with, it's almost entirely keyboard control with the mouse just being used to select dialoge options and move between stations, however the startions can be done with the keyboard as well. But sometimes you just want to use the mouse to actually look at the stations and crew and not go straight into the stations window.

The production value even gets a bit more credit as not only are they all in uniform (Cadet Uniforms, Monster Maroons, Kingon and Romulan Uniforms among others), but one of your crew is an Andorian, a very rarely seen species in this time of Trek production. So probably all brand new cosmetics for this.

It's incredibly tedious with long boring missions that you'll fail and have to do over again several times.

Many old games hold up well today.  This one does not.  It's based on the idea that you should make a game take a long time so the customer feels they got a lot out of it.  That's one part of gaming I'd like to leave in the past.

Another must for Star Trek fans, although this isn't without it's flaws.

The graphics are very 90s (with videos incorporated into the gameplay no less) but everyone (except William Shatner maybe) looks very awkward on 'camera' to me. The crew cutscenes feel like an episode of Friends with bickering and shouting thrown in. 

The controls are pretty dreadful. There are keyboard shortcuts for most things but they don't really tie in with what they do (or are easily confused with something else, especially in the middle of a battle). The worst part is they've somehow made the mouse awkward to use as well. Click zones on the screen are very small and hard to locate. Moving to say the Engineering station usually requires 4 or 5 clicks to find the right spot (there is a keyboard shortcut, no idea what though). Another example is saving and loading your game. About 7 or 8 clicks for that with little feedback from the game about whether you're doing it right or wrong. 

The game difficulty also seems to vary wildly. The first few levels seem incredibly difficult considering their position in the game (the capture the radioactive probe and chase the stolen freighter one took about 50 tries before I got it). But the next few I was blowing up Warbirds and Birds Of Prey like a seasoned pro. 

In summary, if you like ST (especially TOS) then you'll want to play this just because it's ST. They should remake it in TNG timeline with modern graphics and controls etc.

+ The story is interesting and well written. I wish games today had such deep thought put into stories as this game does.
+ The missions are mostly fun, if slightly repetitive (all of them are combat-heavy)
+ The FMV is well directed and the CG was great for the time (the acting though is sometimes a little cheesy)
+ Developing your character and crew's personalities and "scores" over the course of the game via decisions during FMV is brilliant and great fun. If a game did this today in 2022 reviewers would call it revolutionary.
+ Having Walter Koenig, George Takei, and William Shatner really make the story/FMV even more engaging. 
+ The ship UI is great, it models all the stations of the ships with functions that make sense and gel together. 
+ This game actually has a secret final mission that is pretty awesome. Imagine my amazement when replaying in 2022 while following a guide, I discover that if you do all of the dozens of decisions absolutely perfectly throughout the game you're treated to a bonus mission where you get to command the Enterprise. It's kind of crazy all the extra FMV and voice dialogue they recorded for a mission that 99.9% of players probably never saw or even knew existed.

- The biggest downside of this game are that its quite buggy. I had multiple CTDs playing. 
- A few of the missions are also extremely finicky where you can fail by bad luck or poorly explained conditions rather than anything else. Eg, fighting an enemy around a starbase and accidentally hit it once? You'll fail the mission, but won't know until 20 minutes later when you complete all the other objectives first. 
- The combat itself in this game is also ok, not great. The game was rightly criticized upon release of feeling like you're flying a fighter ship rather than a huge starship and I think that's accurate. 
- Related to above, fights against cloaked ships are just tedious and not at all fun as the ships cloak so often that you're essentially flailing around in space, hoping to get a few shots in before they cloak again. And even if you do manage to get a few shots in, they've probably repaired the damage by the time they next decloak. I found the best way to actually win these fights in less than a millennium was to actually ram my ship into theirs which causes massive damage to both ships.

Regardless, for any Star Trek fan this game is definitely worth playing for the FMV alone. I strongly recommend following Navrin's "Complete Walkthrough" guide on Steam. Following it to the letter is realistically the only way you'll ever see the bonus mission. Games were so much more innovative in the 90s.

[h1]“Commanding a starship is your first, best destiny.”
~[i]Captain James T. Kirk[/i][/h1]

Like present times, 90s were a great time to be a [b]Trekkie[/b]. [b]The Next Generation[/b], which started in the late 80s, turned out to be a big hit and the new shows began to appear one after another. There was [b]Benjamin Sisko[/b] taking a stand against the [b]Dominion[/b], there was [b]Kathryn Janeway[/b] leading her crew back home... [i]Man[/i], those were the times! And, of course, there were comics, books and video games. A lot of them. Like... [i]a lot![/i] And it felt [i]awesome[/i]. I mean, there were times when we didn't even have the official games. We had people like [b]Mike Mayfield[/b] and [b]Don Daglow[/b] who used to make unauthorized products. Which, obviously, ended up being on pretty much every computer back then.

90s, on the other hand, marked the whole new era. [b]Simon & Schuster[/b]'s text-based adventures were now left behind and we were starting to get all sorts of entertainment. From legendary [b]25th Anniversary[/b] game and its sequel for personal computers ([b]NES[/b] and [b]Game Boy[/b] versions were not nearly as cool, unfortunately) to a pretty tricky mystery game, in which we were free to explore [b]Terok Nor[/b] ([b]Harbinger[/b]) and even a couple of [b]FMV[/b] games. One about [b]Klingons[/b] (that one even included dictionary, [i]Qapla'![/i]) and one about the [b]Borg[/b].

For us now, though, it's important to remember another game. I'm talking about [b]Interplay[/b]'s [b]Star Trek: Starfleet Academy - Starship Bridge Simulator[/b] for [b]SNES[/b] and [b]SEGA 32X[/b]. Long story short, the game turned us into [b]Starfleet[/b] cadets and let us go through the series of simulations, in which we were supposed to participate in various space operations. We were supposed to tractor things, performing the senor sweeps, looking for peaceful solutions and even re-creating the legendary historical events like [b]Captain Kirk[/b]'s confrontation with [b]USS Reliant[/b] ([b]NCC-1864[/b]), captured by [i]KHAAAAAANNN!!![/i]

Sounds great, right? Unfortunately, the hardware limitations made the game to feel a bit rough and unpleasant here and there. Especially when it's about the [b]SNES[/b] version, but even the one for [b]SEGA 32X[/b] was far from being smooth. If you ever played [b]SNES[/b] version of [b]Chris Roberts[/b]' [b]Wing Commander[/b], you know exactly what I'm talking about. It was still a great game, but... yeah. It was one of those cases, in which [b]PC[/b] mustard race sure had a superior version. Well, technically, [b]3DO[/b] had that weird [b]Super Wing Commander[/b] thingy, but then again, we're not talking 'bout [b]WC[/b] here. Or are we? We'll return to that in a bit, but for now it's important for us to understand that, while [b]WC[/b] was ported on pretty much everything (like that certain game about dragons), [b]Bridge Simulator[/b] never had a [b]PC[/b] counterpart. It was either one console, or another. At least until [b]1997[/b], when [b]Interplay[/b] gave us this. [b]Star Trek: Starfleet Academy[/b].

And before you'll ask, [i]yes[/i], this game is pretty much a new take on good ol' [b]Bridge Simulator[/b] and it follows the same exact formula. Again, you're supposed to become a cadet and participate in those juicy simulations, while you performance there would be rated and make an impact on progression. This time, though, it's more than that. See, [b]Starfleet Academy[/b] is more than just a [b]PC[/b] version of [b]Bridge Simulator[/b]. [b]Interplay[/b] took the next step here and the direction was... pretty obvious, really. Remember when, after [b]Star Wars[/b] proved that space adventures can be really successful on the big screen, [b]Paramount[/b] decided to bring [b]Star Trek[/b] there? Something like that happened here too. Only instead of [b]Star Wars[/b] we've got... Yep, you've guessed it. We've got [b]Wing Commander[/b].

See, [b]WC[/b] was on its top at that time. [b]FMV[/b]-oriented [b]WC III[/b] and [b]IV[/b] changed the entire game with their huge budgets and famous cast (ironically, the role of [b]Maverick[/b] was played by [b]Star Wars[/b]' [b]Mark Hamill[/b]). Naturally, [b]Interplay[/b] decided that they want that too. Especially since they had access to [b]Star Trek[/b] franchise, which already had seven [b]TOS[/b] movies. It was only logical (yes, I'm [b]Vulcan[/b], live long and prosper!) for [b]Interplay[/b] to take their original concept and combine it with [b]WC[/b]. And that's exactly what they did. Did it work? Oh, yes!

Like in [b]WC[/b], our team is our everything now. We won't be able to explore the academy freely (in this case, [b]WC[/b] is a winner), but still, between the missions we'll chill with our guys. Which will be more important than you may think. Just because this game is way more non-linear than [b]WC[/b] and therefore, your decisions may cost you greatly at the end of the game. As a leader of the group, you'll need to be wise. You'll need to understand exactly how to treat people. Otherwise, there'll be... consequences. [b]WC[/b] had that too, but honestly, this game did it better. And, of course, we'll meet our old friends – [b]Kirk[/b], [b]Sulu[/b] and even [b]Chekov[/b]. Unfortunately, [b]Mr. Spock[/b] wasn't included, but hey! Can't have everybody.

Space parts benefited from [b]WC[/b]-like approach too. They became way more dynamic and fast-paced, while also simulating [b]Trek[/b] stuff surprisingly well. See, while the core mechanics here are very [b]WC[/b], the details? The details are all [b]Trek[/b]. You'll need to do everything manually and it feels fantastic! Going on yellow / red alert, controlling the repairs in real time (pretty similar to what we had in [b]MicroProse[/b]'s [b]Star Trek: Generations[/b]), hailing the other vessels and trying to negotiate with them (yes, those negotiations are non-linear too), using the tractor beam, transporter and other juicy things... It feels absolutely amazing. Especially since goals can be pretty complicated too.

This game can be an ass, though. I mean, fighting against cloaked ships is fun ([b]Klingon Birds of Prey[/b]? It's hard not to love 'em), but sometimes, the game will actually punish you for following your orders. I can see why they did it. It's [b]Star Trek[/b] we're talking about. And [b]Star Trek[/b] was always about those moral dilemmas. Like, [b]Kobayashi Maru[/b] anyone? But still, in a computer game format it... can feel unfair here and there. Think 'bout it. You completed your mission. It was hard (the fact that you can't save during the missions doesn't help either), but you made it. You returned to your base and... you learned about how following a certain order was wrong and therefore you've failed. [i]Ouch![/i] Still, this game? It's absolutely beautiful and if you love both [b]Trek[/b] and [b]WC[/b], you should not miss it.

Now, a couple of words about this exact version. It kinda... sucks. For many reasons. First – we've got a regular CD version. Obviously, we won't need to switch CDs, but still, those HQ videos from DVD re-release are not included. Also, don't expect [b]Chekov's Lost Missions[/b]. And while I can see why they didn't bother with HQ videos (those used some weird codec), lack of the addon is just stupid and disappointing. Sure, it's possible to manually add HQ videos from DVD (if you have one that is) and even install the expansion, but honestly, it's all about trial and error and would probably take you some time. And it's just sad, you know? I mean, this version works perfectly fine on [b]Windows 10[/b] / [b]11[/b] and it even has the [b]3dfx[/b] support. Unfortunately, there's no access to it from your [b]Steam[/b] library and the only way to access it is to launch [b]sfad3d.exe[/b] from the game folder (hence lack of play time on my account), but still, it's there. Why didn't they even try to give us all the content? Very illogical and disappointing. Dixi.

This was the first PC game I ever owned and - wow! - does it take me back! I understand why many gamers don't feel that this game matches up to Starfleet Command or Klingon Academy but I was one of the few that thought this was an AMAZING game. Sure, it's dogfighting with Trek ships, but who cares?! 

As a professional composer, I have to make mention this upfront: the soundtrack by Star Trek TNG Allum Ron Jones is exquisite and about as Star Trek as it gets! A huge thumbs up for the sound design too! 

Visually, I always loved the way this game looked. Attention to detail was paid in terms of minute aspects such as the consoles and ship designs. Oh, and kudos for the classic and original TMP era starship additions too! 

The FMV bridge interface is pretty cool (although, admittedly, I always preferred to use the space HUD) and the fact that you can go to each console is nifty. The fact that you'll NEVER use any of the consoles EVER is beside the point, but check out the library console all the same for some interesting easter eggs.

This brings me to the cutscenes and, man-oh-man, is this where the game shines! Nevermind the fact that they got Shatner, Takei and Koenig to reprise their classic roles in a relevant way but the actors playing the protagonist and cadets deliver solid performances! The story presented through the cutscenes could easily have been pitched as a spin-off TV show!

The interactive nature of this game, present in both the cutscenes and the missions, define the fun aspect of this game. There's not one way to complete a single mission. The callback to famous scenarios and episodes/movies even extends the interactivity to allow you to relive classic stories like "Balance of Terror" and "The Wrath of Khan", but with you in the command chair.

Whoever updated the game for Steam did a reasonable job. It's not as smooth and clear as I remember it but it's definitely playable and worth a look, Star Trek fan or not!

In the 90s, Star Trek: Starfleet Academy was heavily anticipated and it was supposed to be best Star Trek game ever. Certainly, it ended being a great game but did not end up meeting the hype and high expectations. Years ago, I bought the physical copy of Starfleet Academy but didn’t realize that a working joystick was essential and all the controls you had to memorize was overwhelming at the time so I gave up on the first mission.

Imagine my excitement when I picked it up on sale recently and now I finally get to give it a second chance. As a big Trek fan, I really enjoyed it. The basic story is you play as cadet on the command track who is working his way through Starfleet Academy by completing a bunch of simulations and at the same time, you must manage all the different personalities of your crew. The game does a good job with its FMV (full motion video) cutscenes which were common in so many 90s games though some of the acting needs improvement. Periodically during these cutscenes, you will have to make several choices which will change the direction of the story and affect your crew’s performance. William Shatner, George Takei and Walter Koenig do a fantastic job reprising their old roles from TOS. 

You could tell the simulations/missions were TOS era “let’s blow them up” as they were really heavy on combat with a bit of diplomacy thrown in on the side. Actually too heavy on combat even for Kirk himself as some missions have you destroying several ships to complete your objective. I would have liked to see a better balance of diplomacy and action. The starships feel too fast but I know Bridge Commander refined what this game tried to do. I really enjoyed being able to play simulations of my favorite episodes/movies like [i]Balance of Terror[/i] and [i]The Wrath of Khan[/i] and even the infamous [i]Kobayashi Maru[/i] scenario. Targeting subsystems was done very well. My main complaint with the simulations is that they do not give you a grade if you pass the mission so I have no idea how well I did (barely passed or aced it) and for a game called Starfleet Academy, grading should be really obvious. 

Overall I highly recommend Starfleet Academy to Star Trek fans especially if you are in the mood for starship combat in the TOS era. I would love to see Steam release the expansion [b]Chekov’s Lost Missions[/b] and [b]Klingon Academy[/b] next.
